- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peaks, especially in early 30d window.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or volatile, model often underestimates or fails to anticipate sharp drops; increase early forecast sensitivity to sentiment dips.
- Model frequently overshoots after recent price spikes (e.g., 2.10+), especially if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive — apply a “cool-down” correction to avoid overreaction.
- If sentiment history shows strong upward momentum (e.g., 3+ consecutive 1.00s), model often overcorrects downward later — adjust for mean reversion bias by slightly dampening late-period forecasts.
- For 30d forecasts, model tends to overestimate early days (1–7) when sentiment is rising, then underestimates later days (15–30) — apply a “sentiment decay” heuristic: reduce forecast magnitude as sentiment stabilizes or turns neutral.
- If sentiment is flat or mixed (0.33–0.67), model often fails to capture mean reversion — use sentiment variance as a proxy for volatility; increase forecast smoothing in such cases.
